sections.heading: Highlights
sections.text: A piezoelectric cantilever with self-adjusting resonant frequency is proposed for harvesting energy and absorbing disturbing torque in rotating environments. The weighted length of the trapezoidal cantilever can be adjusted using the centrifugal force to tune it to its natural frequency. The experimental results indicated that the average output power is approximately $8 2 \mu \mathrm { W }$ for a plate speed range of $2 7 0 { - } 1 2 0 0 \mathrm { r p m }$ . $\bullet$ The weighted cantilever had vibration-absorbing capability between 60 and $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , except fo the region of $1 8 0 \mathrm { H z }$ .

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text: This research aims to develop an energy-harvesting device that converts kinetic energy in rotating environments into electrical energy which can be used as a power source for a tire pressure monitoring system (TPMS) to replace chemical batteries. An energy harvester with a weighted trapezoidal cantilever that had the ability to self-adjust its resonant frequency approaching to the wheel rotation speed to keep a resonant mode in order to generate a higher amount of output power was developed. The weighted length of the trapezoidal cantilever was tuned by the centrifugal force from a rotating wheel to vary the area moment of inertia at the cantilever root. The dynamic equation was derived through the Lagrange method. Moreover, the weighted cantilever can also be considered as a centrifugal pendulum vibration absorber (CPVA) to absorb unexpected vibrations or torque. Therefore, this study analyzed the dynamic behavior of the wheel when a disturbing torque was applied to it. The experimental results revealed that the output power of the prototype was approximately $6 5 \mathrm { - } 1 1 0 \mu \mathrm { W }$ at the wheel rotation speeds in the range of $2 4 0 { - } 1 2 0 0 \ \mathrm { r p m }$ . This demonstrated that the proposed device has the potential to replace the battery in the TPMS. The effective vibration absorption bandwidth of the prototype was approximately $1 3 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , and more than $4 2 \%$ of the vibration absorption ratio was observed under disturbing vibration between $6 0 { - } 1 1 0 \mathrm { H z }$ .

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
According to statistics from National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), 11,000 traffic accidents in the United States were caused by tire failure every year. This prompted NHTSA to establish a Tire Pressure Monitoring System (TPMS) inspection methodology and stipulate all vehicles sold in the United States must install TPMS after 2007. The TPMS displays a warning indicator in the driver's monitor when one or more of the vehicle's tire pressures are abnormal. Most of wireless TPMSs use batteries as the power source; however, the batteries have to be replaced on a regular basis because of their limited lifespan. In the past few years, researches on harvesting energy from rotational environments to supply TPMSs have been proposed [1-5]. The vibration-based energy harvesters are usually designed to work in resonance mode to enhance power generation, but resonant frequencies of a mechanism are usually constant values. Although the energy harvesters based on linear systems have high efficiency only near the resonance, but they are still popular due to their functional simplicity [6]. In order to successfully apply the energy harvesters on a rotating tire, the operating bandwidth of the energy harvesters must be increased. Zhu [7] reviewed recent literatures about increasing the operating frequency range of vibration energy harvesters. There are three main methods to widen the operating bandwidth: tuning the resonant frequency [8, 9], using nonlinear structures [10-13] and bistable structures [14-17]. Bistable structures are a sub-category of the broader nonlinear structures category.

Tuning mechanisms use passive methods to vary the resonant frequency of the energy harvester to match the frequency of the excitation. A passively tunable vibration energy harvester was realized with a sliding mechanism [8]. The sliding mechanism was driven by a centrifugal force to change the tilt angle of the spring which generated a preload on the cantilever. Therefore, the equivalent stiffness of the cantilever can be change to adjust the resonant frequency of the energy harvester. The other tuning mechanism using a trapezoidal piezoelectric cantilever was proposed to harvest rotational energy [9]. The stiffness of the trapezoidal cantilever is adjusted by centrifugal force to tune its resonant frequency. On the other hand, the methods using nonlinear and bistable system to increase operational bandwidth were proposed by researchers. The ability of nonlinear and bistable structures enhances the coupling between the broadband excitation and energy harvesters. Daqaq [10] reviewed the recent researches in the field of nonlinear technique to widen the working bandwidth of energy harvesting devices. This paper highlights the role of nonlinearities in the transduction of energy harvesters under different types of excitations and investigates the conditions, in terms of excitation nature and potential shape, under which such nonlinearities can be beneficial for energy harvesting. The centrifugal stiffening effect was applied to design nonlinear energy harvesters [11, 12]. Using an axial tensile stress caused by the centrifugal force on the cantilever adjusted the stiffness of the cantilever to tune the resonant frequency. Because the centrifugal force is proportional to the square of the rotation speed, the system has a nonlinear characteristic over a range of rotation speeds. With an optimized design, the energy harvester can provide more power in a wide frequency range. A magnetically coupled flextensional rotation energy harvester was proposed [13]. As the excitation magnets rotating, the magnetic force perpendicular to the piezoelectric layer was divided into a pressure and a nonlinear tension force via the flextensional structure, and transmitted to the piezoelectric layer. Harne [14] and Pellegrini [15] reviewed the recent researches in the field of bistable energy harvesters. A structure used the dynamics of an offset pendulum was proposed to increase the operational bandwidth of an energy harvester [16]. The interaction of the proof mass with the piezoelectric beams, and the restoring spring resulted in a double-well potential function characteristic of bistable oscillators. The geometry parameters of the multi-stable configuration altering the potential well depth has been discussed [17]. A piezoelectric bistable buckled beam was proposed [18] to harvest energy from low-speed rotational motion. The rotation of magnets array provided a periodically switching magnetic force to the bistable buckled piezoelectric beam, leading to the snap through motion of the beam and increasing the operational frequency bandwidth with high output power. The performance of a bistable energy harvester is extremely dependent on the magnitude of excitation [10]. If the magnitude of excitation is too small to activate the harvester to oscillate between the double-well potential, the dynamic of bistable will be hindered, and a bistable harvester performs as a monostable one. Compared with a linear system, the nonlinear and bistable system can only bend the frequency-response curve but not increase the amplitude of power. For the TPMS energy harvesters, the vibration source is provided by stable harmonic excitations, so there is no inappropriateness to use the tuning mechanism to widen the operational bandwidth. Moreover, the energy harvesters with tuning mechanisms can keep operating in resonant modes at different excitation frequencies to generate more output power than nonlinear or bistable energy harvesters due to its high quality factor. Considering of the power density and design flexibility, this paper proposed a piezoelectric energy harvester with a trapezoidal cantilever. By using a trapezoidal cantilever, the area moment of inertia can be adjusted by the centrifugal force to tune the resonant frequency of the energy harvester.

With the installation of a device on a rotor, it may generate an eccentric moment to a rotating rotor. Researchers have rarely discussed the kinetic effect of the energy harvester to the rotor. The minimum requirement for a rim-mounted energy harvester is to have no negative kinetic effects on the wheel. Additionally, we hope that the installation of the energy harvester will even have additional vibration absorbing effects to help the wheels to rotate more stable. The other topic of this research is analysis of the energy harvester behaving as a vibration absorber. Many types of vibration absorbers have been developed to reduce the torsional vibrations in a rotating shaft [19-22]. Centrifugal pendulum vibration absorbers (CPVAs) are passive devices used to suppress torsional vibrations in rotating machines [24]. CPVAs consist essentially of pendulums suspended from a rotor such that they can swing in a plane perpendicular to the rotational axis. The vibrations of the rotor cause the pendulum to swing about away its equilibrium position that creates a counteracting torque, this is the basic principle of CPVAs. The major advantage of the CPVAs is that they could absorb vibrations over a range of frequencies. The common methods to model the 2-DOF nonlinear system of CPVAs are Newton's second law of motion [23, 24] and Lagrange equation [25, 26]. Moreover, the stability of CPVA has been analyzed and discussed [27, 28]. With a simple structure and light weight, several applications of CPVAs have been proposed in this half century, and CPVAs have since been employed in vehicle engines [29] and helicopter rotors [30]. The kinetic behavior of a cantilever type energy harvester mounted on the wheel rim could behave as a pendulum. Some cantilever-type [31] and spring-type [32, 33] CPVAs have been proposed.

Summarizing the aforementioned literature review, a weighted trapezoidal piezoelectric cantilever is proposed in this paper for harvesting kinetic energy from a rotating wheel. The cantilever swings reciprocally due to the periodic variation in the tangential component of gravity. With the designed mechanism, the natural frequency of the energy harvester can approach the rotation frequency of the wheel. Consequently, the piezoelectric cantilever swings with a large angle and velocity to obtain the maximum power output. In this research, the vibration-absorption capability of a cantilever-type energy harvester was also analyzed. This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, the dynamic model of the cantilever-type energy harvester mounted on a rolling wheel is derived using the Euler–Lagrange formulation. The design of approximate linear springs and the preliminary numerical results for the cantilever are described in Section 3. In Section 4, the disturbing torque is considered and the kinetic results are provided. The power generation is evaluated in Section 5. In Section 6, the experimental setup, prototype, and experimental procedures are detailed. Moreover, the simulations are compared with the experimental results for specific designs. In Section 7, conclusions are provided.

sections.heading: 2. Dynamic Model of Energy Harvester
sections.text:
As shown in figure 1, a cantilever with a weighted block is fixed on a wheel rim. The distance between the cantilever root and wheel center, radius of the wheel, mass of the cantilever, and mass of the weighted block are represented by $R _ { 2 }$ , $R _ { 1 }$ , $m _ { 1 }$ , and $m _ { 2 }$ , respectively, in figure 1. The weighted length of the cantilever $a$ is defined as the distance between the cantilever root and weighted block. We defined two coordinate systems to describe the model, namely the fixed $( x , y )$ and moving coordinate systems $( { \bar { x } } , { \bar { y } } )$ . The weighted cantilever is deformed repeatedly due to gravitational force, which varied relative to the moving coordinate system. The deflection angle of the cantilever with reference to the fixed coordinate system is defined as $\phi$ . The rotation angle of the wheel and deflection angle of the cantilever with reference to the moving coordinate system are defined as Θ and $\theta$ , respectively.

In our design, the weighted block is directly fixed at the free end of the cantilever, and the tension spring is designed as a beam fixed at both ends. The centrifugal force induced by the I-shaped weighted block is applied to the middle section of the tension spring through the high-modulus polyethylene (HMPE) wire, as displayed in figure 2. The reinforced HMPE wire is used to prevent the cantilever elongated due to the large centrifugal force. The relative displacement between the piezoelectric cantilever and the weight block must be well controlled in [9]. Comparatively to this study, that two degrees-of-freedom design increases the complexity. The weighted block of the proposed energy harvester is fixed with a piezoelectric cantilever, which avoids the uncertainty from the friction force and simplifies the mechanism. Therefore, the effect of the weighted distance and stiffness of the tension spring are also analyzed in this paper. The geometry of the trapezoidal cantilever is illustrated in figure 3.

$\phi , \Theta$ , and $\theta$ have the following relationship:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \phi - \Theta - \theta = \frac { \pi } { 2 } } \end{array}
$$

The coordinates of the wheel center are defined as $( x _ { 0 } , 0 )$ , where $x _ { 0 }$ is the linear movement distance of the wheel. The coordinates of the cantilever root $( x _ { 1 } , y _ { 1 } )$ are defined as follows:

$$
\left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { x _ { 1 } = x _ { 0 } + R _ { 2 } \sin \Theta } \\ { y _ { 1 } = R _ { 2 } \cos \Theta } \end{array} \right.
$$

The cantilever deflection in bending at a specified point is defined as $\delta$ and is expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \delta = \frac { W \bar { x } ^ { 2 } } { 6 E I } ( 3 L - \bar { x } ) } \end{array}
$$

where $L , W , E ,$ , and $I$ are the effective length of the cantilever (defined from its tip to root), force acting on the tip of the beam, modulus of elasticity of the beam, and area moment of inertia of the beam, respectively. $\bar { x }$ is the position on the X-axial of the moving coordinate system. The deflection angle $\theta$ (in radians) at the free end is represented as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \theta = \frac { W L ^ { 2 } } { 2 E I } } \end{array}
$$

Substituting Eq. (4) into Eq. (3), the bending deflection can be rewritten as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \delta = \frac { \theta } { 3 L ^ { 2 } } \bar { x } ^ { 2 } ( 3 L - \bar { x } ) } \end{array}
$$

The coordinates at a specified point of the cantilever are defined as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \left\{ x _ { a } = x _ { 1 } + \bar { x } \sin \Theta + \delta \cos \Theta \right. } \\ { \left\{ y _ { a } = y _ { 1 } + \bar { x } \cos \Theta - \delta \sin \Theta \right. } \end{array}
$$

The velocity components at a specified point of the cantilever are defined as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \left\{ \dot { x } _ { a } = \dot { x } _ { 1 } + \bar { x } \dot { \Theta } \cos \Theta - \delta \dot { \Theta } \sin \Theta + \dot { \delta } \cos \Theta \right. } \\ { \left. \dot { y } _ { a } = \dot { y } _ { 1 } - \bar { x } \dot { \Theta } \sin \Theta - \delta \dot { \Theta } \cos \Theta - \dot { \delta } \sin \Theta \right. } \end{array}
$$

The spring constant of the tension spring is given as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { k _ { s } = \frac { 1 9 2 E _ { s } b _ { s } { h _ { s } } ^ { 3 } } { 1 2 { L _ { s } } ^ { 3 } } } \end{array}
$$

where $E _ { s } , \ b _ { s } , \ h _ { s }$ , and $L _ { s }$ are the modulus of elasticity, width, thickness, and length of the tension spring, respectively. The width at a specific point of the trapezoidal cantilever is determined as follows:

$$
B = b + 2 \beta ( a - \bar { x } )
$$

where $\beta$ and $b$ are the complementary angle of the base angle and tip width of the trapezoidal cantilever, respectively. The weighted length of the cantilever is varied by centrifugal force, and is represented as follows:

$$
a = l _ { i } + ( m _ { 1 } + m _ { 2 } ) R _ { 3 } \dot { \Theta } ^ { 2 } / k _ { s }
$$

where $l _ { i }$ , $( m _ { 1 } + m _ { 2 } ) R _ { 3 } \dot { \Theta } ^ { 2 } / k _ { s }$ , and $R _ { 3 }$ are the initial length of the cantilever when no centrifugal force is applied, displacement of the tension spring, and distance between the equivalent barycenter of the weighted cantilever and wheel center, respectively. The kinetic energy of the cantilever is given as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { T _ { 1 } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \int _ { 0 } ^ { a } \rho h B \big ( \dot { x } _ { a } ^ { 2 } + \dot { y } _ { a } ^ { 2 } \big ) d \bar { x } } \end{array}
$$

where $h$ and $\rho$ are the thickness and density of the cantilever, respectively. The potential energy of the cantilever is given as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { U _ { 1 } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } E \int _ { 0 } ^ { a } I \left( \frac { \partial ^ { 2 } } { \partial \bar { x } ^ { 2 } } \delta \right) ^ { 2 } d \bar { x } + \frac { 1 } { 2 } \int _ { 0 } ^ { a } \rho h B g y _ { a } d \bar { x } } \end{array}
$$

where $g$ is the gravitational acceleration. The kinetic energy of the weighted block is obtained as follows:

$$
T _ { 2 } = { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } m _ { 2 } \left( \dot { X } _ { a } { } ^ { 2 } + \dot { Y } _ { a } { } ^ { 2 } \right) + { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } I _ { 2 } \dot { \phi } ^ { 2 }
$$

where ${ \dot { X } } _ { a }$ and ${ \dot { Y } } _ { a }$ are the velocities of the weighted block at the point $\bar { x } = a$ and $I _ { 2 }$ is the mass moment of inertia of the weighted block. The potential energy of the weighted block is as follows:

$$
U _ { 2 } = m _ { 2 } g Y _ { a }
$$

To analyze the dynamic behavior of the wheel, we incorporated the kinetic and potential energy of the wheel into the model. The kinetic energy of the wheel is as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { T _ { 3 } = \frac 1 2 I _ { w } \dot { \Theta } ^ { 2 } + \frac 1 2 m _ { w } \dot { x _ { 0 } } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}
$$

where $I _ { w }$ is the mass moment of inertia of the wheel and $m _ { w }$ is the mass of the wheel. The potential energy of the wheel $( U _ { 3 } )$ is equal to zero, because no displacement occurs in the y-direction of the wheel. The kinetic and potential energies of the entire system are represented as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { T = T _ { 1 } + T _ { 2 } + T _ { 3 } } } \\ { { \nonumber } } \\ { { U = U _ { 1 } + U _ { 2 } + U _ { 3 } } } \end{array}
$$

The Lagrangian of the entire system is defined as follows:

$$
\mathcal { L } = T - U
$$

The energy dissipation of the weighted cantilever energy harvester is as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { R _ { e } = \frac 1 2 C _ { T } \dot { \phi } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}
$$

where $C _ { T }$ is the overall generalized damping constant of the weighted cantilever energy harvester. The damping constant is given as $C _ { T } = c _ { m } + c _ { e }$ , where $c _ { m }$ is the mechanical damping and $c _ { e }$ is the electrical damping caused by piezoelectric effects. The energy dissipation of the wheel is represented by the following equation:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { R _ { w } = \frac 1 2 c _ { w } \dot { \Theta } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}
$$

where $c _ { w }$ is the overall generalized damping constant of the wheel. In Lagrangian mechanics, the

dynamic equation of the weighted cantilever energy harvester is derived as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \frac { \mathrm { d } } { \mathrm { d t } } \left( \frac { \partial \mathcal { L } } { \partial \dot { \phi } } \right) - \frac { \partial \mathcal { L } } { \partial \phi } + \frac { \partial R _ { e } } { \partial \dot { \phi } } = Q _ { 1 } } \end{array}
$$

where $Q _ { 1 }$ is the nonconservative generalized force corresponding to $\phi$ . The dynamic equation of the wheel is derived as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \frac { \mathrm { d } } { \mathrm { d t } } \left( \frac { \partial \mathcal { L } } { \partial \dot { \Theta } } \right) - \frac { \partial \mathcal { L } } { \partial \Theta } + \frac { \partial R _ { w } } { \partial \dot { \Theta } } = Q _ { 2 } } \end{array}
$$

where $Q _ { 2 }$ is the nonconservative generalized force corresponding to Θ. By substituting Eqs. (1), (2), and (5)–(20) into Eqs. (21) and (22), the dynamic equation of the weighted cantilever energy harvester is derived as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \left( I _ { 2 } + a ^ { 2 } m _ { 2 } + \frac { 1 1 } { 1 0 5 } a ^ { 3 } b h \rho + \frac { 7 } { 1 8 0 } a ^ { 4 } \beta h \rho \right) \ddot { \theta } + \left[ I _ { 2 } + a ^ { 2 } m _ { 2 } + \frac { 1 1 } { 6 0 } a ^ { 3 } b h \rho + \frac { 1 } { 4 } a ^ { 2 } b h \rho R _ { 2 } + a m _ { 2 } R \right] \ddot { \theta } } \\ & { \left. \beta ( \frac { 7 } { 9 0 } a ^ { 4 } h \rho + \frac { 2 } { 1 5 } h a ^ { 3 } \rho R _ { 2 } ) \right] \ddot { \Theta } + \left[ \frac { E h ^ { 3 } ( 2 b + 3 a \beta ) } { 1 8 a } - ( \frac { 1 1 } { 1 0 5 } a ^ { 3 } b h \rho + \frac { 7 } { 1 8 0 } a ^ { 4 } \beta h \rho ) \dot { \Theta } ^ { 2 } \right] \theta + a m _ { 2 } R \dot { \eta } } \\ & { \left[ a m _ { 2 } \sin ( \theta + \Theta ) + ( \frac { 1 } { 4 } a ^ { 2 } b h \rho + \frac { 2 } { 1 5 } a ^ { 3 } \beta h \rho ) \sin \theta \right] g = - C _ { T } \dot { \theta } } \end{array}
$$

Moreover, the dynamic equation of the wheel is derived as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { I _ { w } + I _ { 2 } + a ^ { 2 } m _ { 2 } + m _ { 2 } R _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + 2 a m _ { 2 } R _ { 2 } \cos \theta + \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 3 } a ^ { 3 } b h \rho + a ^ { 2 } b h \rho R _ { 2 } + a b h \rho R _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + \textstyle \frac { 1 1 } { 1 0 5 } a ^ { 3 } h } } \\ { { \ } } \\ { { \displaystyle \langle \frac 1 6 a ^ { 4 } h \rho + \textstyle \frac { 2 } { 3 } a ^ { 3 } h R _ { 2 } \rho + a ^ { 2 } h R _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } \rho + \textstyle \frac { 7 } { 1 8 0 } a ^ { 4 } h \rho \theta ^ { 2 } ) \Big | \ddot { \Theta } + \Big [ I _ { 2 } + a ^ { 2 } m _ { 2 } + a m _ { 2 } R _ { 2 } \cos \theta + \textstyle \frac { 1 1 } { 6 0 } a } } \\ { { \ } } \\ { { a ^ { 2 } b h \rho R _ { 2 } + \beta ( \textstyle \frac { 7 } { 9 0 } a ^ { 4 } h \rho + \textstyle \frac { 2 } { 1 5 } a ^ { 3 } h R _ { 2 } \rho ) \Big ] \ddot { \theta } - a m _ { 2 } R _ { 2 } \sin \theta ( \dot { \theta } ^ { 2 } + 2 \dot { \theta } \dot { \Theta } ) + ( \textstyle \frac { 2 2 } { 1 0 5 } a ^ { 3 } h b \rho + } } \\ { { \ } } \\ { { \ } } \\ { { \textstyle \frac { 7 } { 9 } a ^ { 4 } \beta h \rho ) \theta \dot { \theta } \dot { \Theta } - \Big [ a m _ { 2 } \sin ( \theta + \Theta ) + \Big [ m _ { 2 } R _ { 2 } + \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } a ^ { 2 } b h \rho + a b h \rho R _ { 2 } + \beta ( \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 3 } a ^ { 3 } h \rho + a ^ { 2 } h R _ { 2 } \rho ) } } \\ { { \ } } \\ { { \textstyle \frac 1 4 a ^ { 2 } b h \rho + \textstyle \frac { 2 } { 1 5 } a ^ { 3 } \beta h \rho \cos \Theta \theta \Big ] g = - c _ { w } \dot { \theta } } } \end{array}
$$

To identify a suitable design, the adequately weighted cantilever energy harvester is considered to operate at a constant rotation speed and the dynamic equation of the weighted cantilever energy harvester is linearized by cos $\theta = 1$ and sin $\theta = \theta$ . Eq. (23) is rewritten as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { I _ { t } \ddot { \theta } + C _ { T } \dot { \theta } + \left[ \frac { E h ^ { 3 } ( 2 b + 3 a \beta ) } { 1 8 a } - ( \frac { 1 1 } { 1 0 5 } a ^ { 3 } b h \rho + \frac { 7 } { 1 8 0 } a ^ { 4 } \beta h \rho ) \dot { \Theta } ^ { 2 } + a m _ { 2 } R _ { 2 } \dot { \Theta } ^ { 2 } \right] \theta = 0 } \end{array}
$$

where $I _ { t }$ is the total mass moment of inertia of the weighted cantilever energy harvester, which is represented by the following equation:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { I _ { t } = I _ { 2 } + a ^ { 2 } m _ { 2 } + \frac { 1 1 } { 1 0 5 } a ^ { 3 } b h \rho + \frac { 7 } { 1 8 0 } a ^ { 4 } \beta h \rho } \end{array}
$$

The natural frequency of the weighted cantilever energy harvester is as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \omega _ { n } = \dot { \Theta } \sqrt { \frac { E h ^ { 3 } ( 2 b + 3 a \beta ) } { 1 8 a I _ { t } \dot { \Theta } ^ { 2 } } + \frac { a m _ { 2 } R _ { 2 } - ( \frac { 1 1 } { 1 0 5 } a ^ { 3 } b h \rho + \frac { 7 } { 1 8 0 } a ^ { 4 } \beta h \rho ) } { I _ { t } } } } \end{array}
$$

sections.heading: 3. Numerical Results of Energy Harvester
sections.text:
We solved a quintic equation $\omega _ { n } / \dot { \Theta } = 1$ to obtain the ideal value of $a$ by varying $\dot { \Theta }$ from Eq. (27). There are three real and two complex number solutions of the ideal weighted length of the cantilever are obtained and real number solutions are shown in figure 4. Case 1 is too short to realize. Case 3 is too long and thus is not suitable for this design. Therefore, Case 2 is a reasonable choice for this design. To realize the ideal weighted length in case 2, a nonlinear spring should be designed, but it is difficult to realize. Harvesting energy at high rotation speeds is challenging, especially when an energy harvester is mounted on the wheel rim. This is because high-frequency vibrations are absorbed by the tire. Therefore, we designed a linear spring that approaches to case 2 nonlinear spring in the high rotation speed region, as displayed in figure 5. The slope of this fitting line represents the spring constant of this linear spring, and the intersection between the fitting line and $\mathbf { X }$ -axis indicates the ideal initial length of the cantilever $l _ { i }$ .

To verify the effects of the weighted length adjustment, the frequency ratio is simulated at varying rotation speeds with different initial lengths of the cantilever, as presented in figure 6. The curve for which $l _ { i } = 4$ mm is the closest to $\omega _ { n } / \dot { \Theta } = 1$ when the wheel rotation speed is in the range of 450 to $1 3 5 0 \ \mathrm { r p m }$ . With an adequate weighted length, the area moment of inertia of the trapezoid cantilever can self-adjust its natural frequency to match the rotation frequency of the wheel in a broad frequency range. The frequency ratio is larger at a lower rotation speed because $\dot { \Theta }$ is too small, thus causing the first term in the radical of Eq. (27) to be large.

Figure 7 displays the time domain response of the deflection angle of the cantilever in which $l _ { i } =$ 4 at $4 4 2 . 1 \mathrm { r p m }$ . In this section, a known rotation speed was given to solve the Eq. (23). The maximum value of the deflection angle becomes stable after $_ \mathrm { ~ 6 ~ s ~ }$ , and the maximum deflection angle of the cantilever is approximately $4 0 ^ { \circ }$ . Figure 8 presents the variations in the deflection angle of the cantilever versus the wheel rotation speed with different initial lengths. The peaks in figure 8 demonstrates that the cantilever resonation is occurred. For the design in which $l _ { i } = 4$ , two peaks appear at 274 and $1 2 4 7 \mathrm { r p m }$ corresponding to the two intersections presented in figure 5. For the designs in which $l _ { i } <$ 4, the deflection angle of the cantilever decreases rapidly beyond the resonant frequency. For the designs in which $l _ { i } > 4$ , the deflection angle of the cantilever decreases monotonically with the rotation speed of the wheel because the frequency ratio do not achieve to 1 in these rotation speeds. Figure 9 presents the maximum angular velocity of the cantilever varies with the rotation speed of the wheel at different initial lengths of the cantilever. The design with $l _ { i } = 4$ has the widest operating bandwidth for the largest angular velocity, because the frequency ratio is approximately equal to 1 when the rotation speed is in the range of 274–1247 rpm. When an adequate initial length is decided, the cantilever provides large kinetic energy in the widest frequency range as a self-adjusting energy harvester.

sections.heading: 4. Disturbing Torque Absorption
sections.text:
This section analyzes the dynamic behavior of the wheel by solving equations pertaining to the motion of the wheel. The disturbing torque could be induced from bearing defects in the axle. Bearing defects include the damage of inner ring, outer ring and balls. The frequency of vibration caused by damaged bearings is approximately 2 to 8 times the rotational frequency of the wheel. We applied a disturbing torque on the wheel and observed the vibration of the wheel with and without a weighted cantilever. The disturbing torque is in the following form:

$$
T _ { q } = T _ { 0 } + T _ { a l } \sin \omega _ { t } t
$$

where $T _ { 0 }$ is a constant torque, and $T _ { a l }$ sin $\omega _ { t } t$ is a disturbing torque with amplitude $T _ { a l }$ and frequency $\omega _ { t }$ . In the steady state, the motion of the wheel is assumed to be of the following form:

$$
\begin{array} { l } { \Theta = \Omega t + \Phi _ { p } } \\ { { \dot { \Theta } } = \Omega + { \dot { \Phi } } _ { p } } \\ { { \ddot { \Theta } } = { \ddot { \Phi } } _ { p } } \end{array}
$$

where $\Omega$ is the steady rotation speed and $\Phi _ { p }$ is the oscillating amplitude of the wheel. The first and second time derivatives of $\Phi _ { p }$ represent the angular velocity and acceleration of the wheel’s oscillation, respectively. By substituting Eqs. (28)–(31) into Eq. (23) and Eq. (24), the two equations of the system can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { { } + a ^ { 2 } m _ { 2 } + \frac { 1 1 } { 1 0 5 } a ^ { 3 } b h \rho + \frac { 7 } { 1 8 0 } a ^ { 4 } \beta h \rho \bigg ) \ddot { \theta } + \Big [ I _ { 2 } + a ^ { 2 } m _ { 2 } + \frac { 1 1 } { 6 0 } a ^ { 3 } b h \rho + \frac { 1 } { 4 } a ^ { 2 } b h \rho R _ { 2 } + a m _ { 2 } R _ { 2 } \rho ^ { 2 } \Big ] \stackrel { \triangledown } { \theta } = 0 , } \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { ( \frac { \gamma } { 9 0 } a ^ { 4 } h \rho + \frac { 2 } { 1 5 } h a ^ { 3 } \rho R _ { 2 } ) \Big | \ddot { \Phi } _ { p } + \left[ \frac { E h ^ { 3 } ( 2 b + 3 a \beta ) } { 1 8 a } - ( \frac { 1 1 } { 1 0 5 } a ^ { 3 } b h \rho + \frac { 7 } { 1 8 0 } a ^ { 4 } \beta h \rho ) ( \Omega + \dot { \Phi } _ { p } ) ^ { 2 } \right] \theta + } } \\ { { \ } } \\ { { m _ { 2 } R _ { 2 } \sin \theta \left( \Omega + \dot { \Phi } _ { p } \right) ^ { 2 } - \left[ a m _ { 2 } \sin ( \theta + \Omega t + \Phi _ { p } ) + ( \frac { 1 } { 4 } a ^ { 2 } b h \rho + \frac { 2 } { 1 5 } a ^ { 3 } \beta h \rho ) \sin \theta \right] g = - \frac { 1 } { 1 0 } \Omega \cos ( \Omega + \Omega t ) . } } \end{array}
$$

and

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \left[ I _ { w } + I _ { 2 } + a ^ { 2 } m _ { 2 } + m _ { 2 } R _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + 2 a m _ { 2 } R _ { 2 } \cos \theta + \frac { 1 } { 3 } a ^ { 3 } b h \rho + a ^ { 2 } b h \rho R _ { 2 } + a b h \rho R _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + \frac { 1 1 } { 1 0 5 } \right] \sin \theta } } \\ { { \ } } \\ { { \beta ( \frac { 1 } { 6 } a ^ { 4 } h \rho + \frac { 2 } { 3 } a ^ { 3 } h R _ { 2 } \rho + a ^ { 2 } h R _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } \rho + \frac { 7 } { 1 8 0 } a ^ { 4 } h \rho \theta ^ { 2 } ) \left[ \tilde { \eta } _ { p } + \left[ I _ { 2 } + a ^ { 2 } m _ { 2 } + a m _ { 2 } R _ { 2 } \cos \theta + \frac { 2 } { 1 0 5 } a ^ { 2 } h \rho \right] \right] \sin \theta } } \\ { { \ } } \\ { { \frac { 1 } { 4 } a ^ { 2 } b h \rho R _ { 2 } + \beta ( \frac { 7 } { 9 0 } a ^ { 4 } h \rho + \frac { 2 } { 1 5 } a ^ { 3 } h R _ { 2 } \rho ) \left[ \tilde { \eta } - a m _ { 2 } R _ { 2 } \sin \theta ( \dot { \theta } ^ { 2 } + 2 \dot { \theta } ( \Omega + \Phi _ { p } ) ) + ( \frac { 2 2 } { 1 0 5 } a ^ { 5 } h \rho - \rho A \rho ) \right] \sin \theta } } \\ { { \ } } \\ { { \frac { 7 } { 9 0 } a ^ { 4 } \beta h \rho ) \theta \dot { \theta } ( \Omega + \Phi _ { p } ) - \left[ a m _ { 2 } \mathrm { S i n } \big ( \theta + \Omega t + \Phi _ { p } \big ) + \left[ m _ { 2 } R _ { 2 } + \frac { 1 } { 2 } a ^ { 2 } b h \rho + a b h \rho R _ { 2 } + \frac { 1 } { 1 0 5 } a ^ { 2 } h \rho \right] \cos \theta \right]} } \\ { { \ } } \\   \beta \left( \frac { 1 } { 3 } a ^ { 3 } h \rho + a ^ { 2 } h R _ { 2 } \rho \right)  \sin \Theta + \left( \frac { 1 } { 4 } a ^ { 2 } b h \rho + \frac { 2 } { 1 5 } a ^ { 3 } \beta h \rho \right) \cos ( \Omega t + \Phi _ { p } ) \theta \left[ g - { \tau _ { w } } ( \rho A \rho ) \right] \sin ( \Omega t + \Omega t - \rho A \ \end{array}
$$

The oscillation amplitudes of the wheel mounted with and without an adequately weighted cantilever at two different rotation speeds are presented in figure 10. The effect of the wheel rotation speed on the oscillation amplitude is not very significant because the disturbing frequency is considerably higher than the rotation frequency of the wheel. However, there is an evident reduction in the oscillation amplitude of the wheel when the adequately weighted cantilever is employed. According to the law of conservation of energy, converting the kinetic energy of the wheel into electrical energy inevitably causes the kinetic energy of the wheel to reduce. Thus, the vibration in the tangential direction of the wheel can be reduced due to the installation of the energy harvester, both figures 10 and 11 revealed this phenomenon.

To quantify the effect of vibration absorption, we defined the dimensionless absorption ratio as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \eta _ { a b } = \frac { \Phi _ { w i t h } } { \Phi _ { w i t h o u t } } } \end{array}
$$

where $\Phi _ { w i t h }$ and $\Phi _ { w i t h o u t }$ are the oscillation amplitudes of the wheel mounted with and without an adequately weighted cantilever, respectively. When the absorption ratio is less than 1, the adequately weighted cantilever has the vibration absorption ability and can reduce the oscillation amplitude of the wheel caused by the disturbing torque. In figure 11, the absorption ratio is plotted against the disturbing frequency at wheel rotation speeds of 191, 477 and $9 5 5 ~ \mathrm { r p m }$ . The difference in the rotation speed determines the frequency at which vibration absorption begins. The case that has the low rotation speed $( 1 9 1 \mathrm { r p m } )$ begins to absorb the vibration at a lower disturbing frequency than the case that has a higher rotation speed $( 9 5 5 ~ \mathrm { r p m } )$ . By using an appropriate design in which $l _ { i } = 4 ~ \mathrm { ~ m m }$ , the oscillation amplitude of the wheel caused by the disturbing torque at $9 5 5 ~ \mathrm { r p m }$ can be reduced by more than $5 0 \%$ for a disturbing frequency in the range of 9 to $1 5 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . The peak appears at $1 8 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ is the resonant frequency of the wheel after installing the adequately weighted cantilever.

sections.heading: 5. Power Generation Evaluation
sections.text:
Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) films were attached to the surface of the cantilever to transfer electrical power. According to the piezoelectric equivalent circuit, the relationship between the output voltage across the external resistive load and the strain rate of the cantilever is represented by the following equation:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \dot { V } = \frac { 2 t _ { c } d _ { 3 1 } E _ { p } } { F _ { s p } \varepsilon _ { p } } \dot { S } - \frac { 1 } { R C _ { b } } V } \end{array}
$$

where $t _ { c }$ , $d _ { 3 1 }$ , $E _ { p }$ , and $\varepsilon _ { p }$ are thickness, piezoelectric strain coefficient, Young’s modulus, and dielectric constant of the PVDF, respectively. $F _ { s p }$ represents the series or parallel coefficient. If the two layers of the device are wired in series, then $F _ { s p } = 1$ . If the two layers of the device are wired in parallel, then $F _ { s p } = 2$ . The electrical damping of a piezoelectric generator with a resistive load $R$ is derived as follows [9]:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { c _ { e } = R \left( i _ { s } \frac { h } { a } - C _ { b } \frac { \dot { V } } { \dot { \theta } } \right) ^ { 2 } } \end{array}
$$

where $i _ { s } = F _ { s p } a B d _ { 3 1 } E _ { p }$ . By substituting Eq. (36) into Eq. (23) and simultaneously solving Eqs. (23) and (35), the output voltage of the PVDF can be obtained.

The output voltage and power of the monolayer PVDF is plotted against the rotation speed of the wheel with different initial lengths of the cantilever, as displayed in figure 12. By using a monolayer PVDF in the cantilever connected to a $2 2 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ resistor, the adequately weighted cantilever with $l _ { i } = 4$ mm generates higher power than other initial length designs in the rotation range of 300 to $1 2 0 0 \mathrm { r p m }$ . The mechanical damping value was estimated at $1 . 0 \mathrm { N - s / ( k g - m ) }$ from the free vibration.

sections.heading: 6. Experimental Results
sections.text:
To conduct the experiment, a wheel emulator was set up, as shown in figure 13 (a). The emulator comprised a rotatable plate driven by an AC servo motor (MHMD0821P, Panasonic) that was connected to a PC with a motion control card (DMC-1412, Galil). In the case of constant car speed, the wheel behaved the same as the rotatable plate, so the wheel was replaced by a rotatable plate in the experiment. The NI LabVIEW software and the NI USB-9234 DAQ device was used to digitalize the output voltage of the PVDF, and the acceleration was measured by the accelerometer to facilitate computer compilation. A multi-channel slip ring made by Asiantool was mounted at the center of the rotatable plate to transfer the signal from rotating parts to a fixed platform. A prototype of the weighted piezoelectric cantilever energy harvester is presented in figure 13 (b). The adjustable screws on the weighted block were used to change the centroid position of the weighted block in order to fine adjust the distance of the weighted length while conducting the experiment. The length the weighted block is $6 0 \mathrm { m m }$ and the length of the piezoelectric cantilever is $4 \mathrm { m m }$ . These dimensions are compatible with those of a TPMS module. The weight of the weighted cantilever without a frame is $7 . 9 \ \mathrm { g } \cdot$ , which is less than the weight of a lithium battery $( 9 \ \mathrm { g } )$ in TPMS.

There were two different settings in the experiment. The spring constant and initial weighted length in Setting 1 were $1 0 5 7 6 8 \ \mathrm { N / m }$ and $4 . 0 2 \ \mathrm { m m }$ , respectively. In Setting 2, relatively, these parameters were $1 0 9 8 8 6 \ \mathrm { N / m }$ and $3 . 9 9 \mathrm { m m }$ , respectively. The ideal operation region of the proposed design (setting 2) is $3 0 { \mathrm { - } } 1 3 0 \ \mathrm { k m / h }$ , which was determined based on normal the driving speeds of cars. The experimental and simulated results of the output voltage versus the rotation speed for these two settings consisting of a monolayer PVDF film are shown in figure 14. With Setting 2, the peaks appeared at 240 and $1 2 0 0 \mathrm { r p m }$ ; this implies that the system resonated with the rotation speed at these two frequencies. The two output voltage peaks in the experimental result appeared approximately 30 rpm $[ 0 . 5 \mathrm { H z } ]$ ) earlier than the simulation result. The experimental results of these two cases verified the correctness of the physical model. Both the numerical and experimental results demonstrate that the operation bandwidth can be changed by different initial weighted lengths. The experimental results of the output voltage and power versus the rotation speed for these two settings consisting of a four-layer PVDF film were presented in figure 15. These four layers were wired in parallel and connected with an external resistance of $6 0 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ according to impedance matching at rotation speed of $5 3 9 \mathrm { r p m }$ (60 $\mathrm { { k m / h } }$ car speed). That speed is a medium value in the experiment. Setting 2 behaved as wider bandwidth than Setting 1. That is because the $l _ { i }$ of Setting 2 makes the ratio of $\omega _ { n } / \dot { \Theta }$ approaches to one. The average output power on the external resistance of Setting 2 in the plate speed range of 270 to 1200 rpm was approximately $8 2 \mu \mathrm { W } .$ The power consumption of TPMS is $2 0 \mu \mathrm { W }$ [16], which is one-fourth of the power generation of the proposed device, making the proposed device adequate as the power source for TPMS.

A shaker consisted of an eccentric motor was mounted on the rotatable plate to generate vibration. The vibration induced tangential torque that is seemed as disturbing torque. The vibration acceleration in the tangential direction of the rotatable plate was measured using an accelerometer (352C65, PCB). The accelerometer was used to measure the acceleration of vibration of the rotatable plate instead of the amplitude during simulation without the loss of meaning. The experimental and simulation results of the absorption ratio at a plate rotation speed of 477 rpm using the adequately weighted cantilever (Setting 2) are shown in figure 16. The vibration absorption ratio was more than $4 2 \%$ for frequency range from 60 to $1 1 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . Moreover, the adequately weighted cantilever had a vibration absorbing effect between 60 to $2 0 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ except for close to $1 8 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ that is resonant frequency contributed by the plate and energy harvester. The difference between the experimental and the simulation result is due to the difference in the vibration generation source and damping factor. The resonance of the adequately weighted cantilever occurred at the disturbing frequency of $1 8 0 \mathrm { H z }$ is the same as the simulation result.

sections.heading: 7. Conclusions
sections.text:
In this paper, a novel weighted self-tuning energy harvester with a trapezoidal cantilever attached with PVDF films is proposed for use in rotational environments. From the dynamic models, we determined that the weighted length of the weighted cantilever should be adjusted using centrifugal force to vary the area moment of inertia at the root of the cantilever. This ensures that the natural frequency of the energy harvester matches the wheel rotation frequency. The simulation results revealed that by using adequate design parameters, the energy harvester could effectively increase the operation frequency range for hight output power. The weighted length of the cantilever was crucial. The experimental results indicated that the average output power was $8 2 \mu \mathrm { W }$ for a car with speed in the range of $2 7 { - } 1 3 6 ~ \mathrm { k m / h }$ , which covers the normal driving speed. Thus, the adequately weighted energy harvester could replace chemical batteries and be utilized as a power source for the TPMS, which has an average power requirement of $2 0 \mu \mathrm { W }$ .

The weighted cantilever was also considered to be a CPVA, and the vibration-absorption phenomenon of the weighted cantilever was analyzed. We applied a disturbing torque on the wheel to analyze the effect of vibration absorption between the oscillation amplitude of the wheel with and without the adequately weighted cantilever. The experimental results revealed that the optimal vibration-absorption frequency range of the adequately weighted cantilever was $6 0 { - } 1 1 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , and more than $5 8 \%$ of the vibration was absorbed. The effective vibration-absorption bandwidth of the prototype was approximately $1 3 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . Therefore, by using an apppropriate design, the adequately weighted cantilever could simultaneously generate power and absorb disturbing torque. A nonuniform trapezoid cantilever that can expand the design space to match the natural frequency will be considered in the future.

Yu-Jen Wang was born in Tainan, Taiwan, in 1977. He received his Ph.D. from Department of Power Mechanical Engineering at National Tsing Hua University, Taiwan, in 2011.
